questions.q: What is the definition of imagery in literature? List the five senses it can appeal to.
questions.a: Imagery is the use of descriptive language that appeals to the five senses — sight, sound, smell, touch, and taste — to create vivid mental pictures. A wrong answer (e.g., "imagery means pictures in a book") reveals the student confuses the literary term with visual illustrations and misses the sensory dimension.

questions.q: In the chapter, the author writes: "ओक़बज़ ओक्कज़ उस्के तय दक्स चमस फोफपकु <अक्स लेसवर्ह गस — रच हि तस ओक्कज़ घि उस्के!" Explain in your own words what this metaphor suggests about the salt pan and the natural process of evaporation.
questions.a: The metaphor suggests that the salt pan acts like an efficient, almost intentional machine that separates salt from water even without the sun's direct heat, highlighting the ingenuity of the Agariyas' traditional method. A wrong answer (e.g., "it means the salt pan is hot") shows the student takes the metaphor literally and misses the comparison between the pan and a purposeful separator.

questions.q: Find one example of tactile imagery (related to touch) from the text and explain how it helps the reader experience the physical conditions of the salt workers.
questions.a: Example: "क्लकस्यह ंक्सवह ढककक ढककक ढकक" (the description of the salt crust being hard like a hoof). This tactile image lets the reader feel the hardness and unevenness of the salt surface underfoot, conveying the physical strain on workers' feet. A wrong answer that picks a visual image ("white salt flats") shows the student cannot distinguish sensory modalities.

questions.q: Compare the metaphors "उसफर-उसफर तसलक ओक़कन इसपहन्क एकेक गस" (mirage-like illusion) and "ओक़बज़ ओक्कज़ उस्के तय दक्स..." (salt pan separates salt from water). How do these two metaphors create contrasting impressions of the salt pan landscape?
questions.a: The first metaphor portrays the salt pan as an elusive, dreamlike mirage — beautiful but intangible — while the second portrays it as a practical, grounded tool that reliably extracts salt. Together they capture the dual nature of the Rann: a harsh, illusory landscape that is also a site of real, skilled labor. A wrong answer that treats both as mere descriptions misses the contrast between illusion and utility.

questions.q: The author calls the salt pan "फुथ वस लककज़तफुद लइफकक दक फोहककतु दुस ओकह जस[क्क ओक़बज़ उस्के एकेक इसा चमस फोफपकु <अक्स फेव तकरह गस" (a raw narrator of history and geography). Evaluate whether this metaphor is effective in conveying the chapter's central theme. Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, it is effective because the salt pan literally contains layers of history (generations of Agariyas) and geography (the Rann's unique ecology) in its crystals, and the metaphor elevates a simple evaporation bed to a storyteller. A weak evaluation (e.g., "it's a nice metaphor") without textual evidence shows the student cannot critique literary devices against thematic purpose.

questions.q: Write a short paragraph (4-5 lines) describing a monsoon evening in your city using at least two types of imagery and one original metaphor (do not copy from the text).
questions.a: A good answer will include, e.g., auditory imagery (rain drumming on tin roofs), olfactory imagery (wet earth smell), and a metaphor like "the streets turned into mirrors reflecting the city's lights". A poor answer uses only visual imagery and a clichéd metaphor ("rain like tears"), showing limited sensory range and derivative thinking.
